question: An events team wants a wide field of ideas for a member engagement campaign before narrowing down. Which two prompt choices best suit this brainstorming stage? Select two.
options: A) Ask for the single strongest idea straight away so the team can start work sooner.
B) Provide one finished campaign write-up and ask for close variations on that model.
C) State the limits any idea must respect, such as a small budget and six weeks.
D) Fix the tone, house style and final format so every idea arrives ready to publish.
E) Ask for a spread of clearly different directions, each given a short label and a line.
correct_answers: C) State the limits any idea must respect, such as a small budget and six weeks.
E) Ask for a spread of clearly different directions, each given a short label and a line.
explanations: Jumping to one recommendation skips the divergent step entirely, and it hides the alternatives the team asked for precisely so they could compare them.
Anchoring on a finished example narrows the output to near-copies, which is useful when matching a template but counterproductive when seeking range.
Correct. Constraints serve a different purpose from breadth: they keep the wide field usable by excluding options the team could never actually run.
Publication-ready styling belongs to the drafting stage. Applied now it wastes effort on ideas that will mostly be discarded and slows the divergent pass.
Correct. Brainstorming values coverage over polish. Short labelled options let the team scan a wide field cheaply, which polished prose actively discourages.
